doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Back to New York in 1960 and the rebel Newport festival
summary: Ware pawns the fiddle, rides back with Walter Perkins, then plays the Jazz Artists counter-festival at Newport; the group folds.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: It don't make sense. Then, on top of that, you got to keep up your other dues at your home local. But that's the way it went down. Anyway, they got me fined, and Johnny Griffin had a week at the Regal, a big band, you know, he wanted me to come in with him. But they wouldn't let me play. So I'm stuck in Chicago; I can't work, and I wound up pawning the fiddle that he bought me; started bumming around, drinking and carrying on. And I stayed out there until I just got tired, and in the summer of 1960, Walter Perkins,* drummer who came to New York in the late fifties with MJO plus 2 -- Bob Cranshaw, Hal Mabern Al Maybal and Willie ... oh, the trumpet player, (Thomas - ed.) Dennis or something like that -- and George Coleman I believe; no, Frank Strozier Storchin was on alto. And anyway, he was going back to New York and he said, "Come on, ride drive with me, Wilbur." So I left, and this was just before the Newport Festival in 1960. I get back to New York with him; we pulled in; Joe Termini and his brother had the Five Prior Spot as well as the Jazz Gallery, so we pulled up in front of that, and that's where he let me out. I was with the clothes on my back, and I found someplace to crash that night, and I ran into Alan Allen

Eager, a tenor player, a white boy -- and they were getting a bunch of groups together to go and play Newport, and Max's Ornette's group and Arnett's group, Coleman Hawkins, Old Man Joe Jones, Kenny Dorham, King Durham, Kenny Drew, Arthur Taylor, Abdul-Malik, Baby Lawrence, the dancer.

We had what they called, they defined it and nicknamed it a 'Rump Sale' and they decided on a name that The Jazz Artists give. They were against something about Wein Lorillard, George and Loreli, you know, the owners of the Newport Festival -- excluding certain groups, you know. If you weren't in the 'in' groups, you didn't get a chance to play Newport. That's what Mingus' whole thing was. MS. : It's still the same way.

Yeah. So Mingus Amos was up there and Arnett, and he had a cite called the Cliffwalk Manor, a beautiful hotel right there overlooking the beaches and whatnot, the big grounds where they had tents set up, and we were playing, all day having our little thing and charging admission to get in, and it was beautiful.

Then all of a sudden, that riot started. And oh boy, that broke up the Newport thing. But we come back to New York, and they got a theatre over on the east side, that the Jazz Artists give, and we were gonna play jazz concerts nightly, you know, but we couldn't get no publicity, nobody to handle us, you know? I don't know who it had leaked to, the word had
come out and nobody would touch us. So the act folded.
